newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba shuns political strings to hurricane aid.
newsitem.headline: Cuba shuns political strings to hurricane aid.

text.p: Cuban authorities, expecting emergency aid donated by Cubans living in the United States for victims of Hurricane Lili, said on Thursday there should be no political strings to the assistance.
Jose Cabanas, a Foreign Ministry official, said aid could come only through established channels and according to international norms, with "no political overtones."

Washington said Wednesday it had waived a ban on direct flights from the United States to Cuba to allow a Roman Catholic Church charity, Caritas Cubana, to send a planeload of food to the communist-ruled island.
Caritas Cubana said the plane would fly later this week to Cienfuegos, one of the areas worst hit by the hurricane, with 78 metric tons of food.

Cabanas, quoted by the Cuban news agency Prensa Latina, said Cuba could tell the difference between Cubans in the United States who wanted to help their families and those who wanted to "manipulate" the situation and use it for political ends.
Caritas Cubana director Rolando Suarez said the Communist Party's religious affairs office had made clear no aid could be stamped or marked with political slogans.
Some Cuban Americans, mostly in Florida, have mobilised to send aid to Cuba but others are against donations on the grounds that they would help prop up President Fidel Castro's government.
Hurricane Lili destroyed more than 5,000 homes, caused widespread damage to crops and cut power lines and communicantions in central and western areas of Cuba.
Mexico was the first country to deliver aid, sending two planeloads of food and roofing material. Spain has also promised emergency assistance worth $200,000.
The Cuban government has appealed to the United Nations for humanitarian assistance. Caritas has also appealed internationally for aid.
